tasks.freeTitle: Can the site run for free?

freeVerdict.freeExceptDomain: Yes, apart from the domain. Every service is on a free plan today and nothing costs anything monthly. The .ro domain is paid yearly and is the one certain expense.
freeVerdict.freeButAtALimit: Yes, but today's email allowance is spent. Nothing is lost — the messages go out after midnight UTC. If you open registration now, the confirmations arrive tomorrow morning.
freeVerdict.notFree: Caution, though not necessarily a breach. A published event is marked as charging a fee. Vercel's Hobby terms do not look at legal form — being an NGO is not an exemption, and the word “non-profit” does not appear in them at all. Two things do matter: “Asking for Donations does not fall under commercial usage” (their own explicit note), but “advertising the sale of a product or service” does. So a contribution presented as a donation is fine; a mandatory entry fee is not, even when it only covers costs. This site takes no money and has no payment integration — that helps, but it is not the only test.

tasks.registrationsLeftToday: {sent} of {allowance} messages have gone out today. That leaves room for roughly {count} complete registrations — a floor, not a ceiling, because somebody who lands on the waiting list costs more messages.
tasks.limitsIntro: Not every documented limit — the four this club will actually meet, plus the rule about money. “Applies” means you are under it; “reached” means it is biting today.

mailgunDaily.title: 100 messages a day, which is about 33 registrations
mailgunDaily.body: Mailgun's free plan sends 100 messages a day, and one completed registration costs three: confirm your address, sign the declaration, registration confirmed. A race opening entries to a hundred people crosses it before lunch. Messages past the cap are not lost — they wait until after midnight UTC.

schedulerFloor.title: The scheduler fires about every two hours, not every five minutes
schedulerFloor.body: Vercel Hobby allows one scheduled run a day and refuses a finer expression at deploy time, so the scheduler is a GitHub Actions workflow plus an external pinger. Measured on this repository, Actions alone fires roughly every two hours. That delays a message rather than losing it — but a confirmation arriving two hours late, on registration day, is experienced as a broken site.

commercialUse.title: Vercel Hobby requires non-commercial use — the club sells nothing
commercialUse.body: Brașov Runners sells nothing and takes no money, and this site has no payment integration at all. Of Vercel's five examples of commercial usage, four do not touch us: we request no payments, advertise the sale of nothing, carry no affiliate links and run no advertisements. One remains and it does not depend on what the club does: “receiving payment to create, update, or host the site”. If anyone is ever paid to work on this site, that alone is commercial usage — it is the single thing worth watching here. For anything resembling an entry contribution: Vercel states explicitly that “Asking for Donations does not fall under commercial usage”, so a donation is fine, while a mandatory fee would fall under “advertising the sale of a service”.

identityDomain.title: Staff sign-in on the club's own domain needs a paid plan
identityDomain.body: Zitadel Free includes zero custom domains and one identity administrator. While staff sign in on the provider's hostname, neither matters. From the day the club's domain is bound, both do.

orgRepository.title: A club-owned repository forces a paid Vercel plan
orgRepository.body: Vercel Hobby cannot connect to a Git organization's repository, only to a personal one. The club wants the repository in its own name — which forces paid Vercel or a move to the fallback host. Two things the club wants that block each other.

tasks.plansTitle: What we are on, and what the next step up costs
tasks.plansIntro: Prices are quoted from the project's own documentation, checked on {checked}. Vendors change them without notice — re-check before spending anything.

domain.name: .ro domain
domain.freeGives: The one certain expense and the only line with no free option. Paid yearly, at the registrar's price.

mailgun.name: Mailgun (email)
mailgun.freeGives: Free: 100 messages a day, 5 authorized sandbox recipients, one day of log retention.

vercel.name: Vercel (hosting)
vercel.freeGives: Hobby: 100 GB bandwidth, 1M invocations, one scheduled run a day, non-commercial only.

neon.name: Neon (database)
neon.freeGives: Free: 0.5 GB storage, 100 CU-hours a month, 5 GB egress.

zitadel.name: Zitadel (staff sign-in)
zitadel.freeGives: Free: 100 daily active users, one administrator, no custom domain.

githubActions.name: GitHub Actions (scheduler)
githubActions.freeGives: Free and unlimited on a public repository. On a private one, 2,000 minutes a month.

tasks.bumpTitle: What to bump temporarily, and when to drop it again
tasks.bumpIntro: A plan nobody drops again is the expensive failure here, and no dashboard will remind you. Write the downgrade date wherever you wrote the upgrade date. Bump one thing, watch, then the next — two at once means never learning which one was binding.

mailgun.when: You expect more registrations than the daily allowance covers
mailgun.what: Mailgun Basic, $15/month, removes the daily limit entirely and includes 10,000 messages a month.
mailgun.back: Drop it the month after: one month per race, not a standing subscription.

neon.when: Pages are slow, or the database returns connection errors
neon.what: Neon Launch, usage-based, no monthly minimum.
neon.back: Drop it once the registration window closes.

vercelLoad.when: Vercel throttles the site under traffic
vercelLoad.what: Vercel Pro, $20/month for each person who deploys. Viewer seats are free.
vercelLoad.back: Drop it only if it was taken purely for load. Note: exceeding a Hobby cap pauses the feature for 30 days and you cannot buy your way out — upgrade before the window, never during it.

vercelCommercial.when: The club starts charging entry, or the repository moves to a club organization
vercelCommercial.what: Vercel Pro, or the move to the fallback host already decided.
vercelCommercial.back: Not dropped. This is not a traffic spike, it is a change in what the site is.

Devs.title: This deployment's configuration
Devs.intro: What is configured here and what is missing. Variable names and whether they have a value — never the value.
Devs.neverValues: No value, key or secret appears on this page. Only the variable's name and whether it is set.
Devs.runtimeIntro: What the database and the scheduled jobs report at this moment. The same values as /api/health.

overall.limited: Working, but doing less than you probably expect. See the marked items below.
overall.blocked: Something this deployment needs in order to start, or to work, is missing. See the red items below.

emailCaptureLocal.title: Email
emailCaptureLocal.body: Messages are kept in memory and go nowhere. The only mode local and test accept.

emailCaptureDeployed.title: Email
emailCaptureDeployed.body: Messages are kept in memory and go nowhere — and on a hosted environment nobody can read them, because the process is gone. Anyone registering here never receives the confirmation. For real delivery: EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE=allowlist, together with EMAIL_ALLOWLIST and the three Mailgun variables.

emailAllowlist.title: Email
emailAllowlist.body: Transmits only to the addresses in EMAIL_ALLOWLIST; everything else is captured. Each address must also be an authorized recipient in Mailgun, spelled exactly the same.

emailLive.title: Email
emailLive.body: Transmits to anybody. Permitted in production only.

staffProvider.title: Staff sign-in
staffProvider.body: Through the identity provider. Who may in is still decided by the staff_users table, not by the provider.

staffDevSwitcher.title: Staff sign-in
staffDevSwitcher.body: Development identities, local and test only. Not real people.

staffDisabled.title: Staff sign-in
staffDisabled.body: There is no way in at all: every staff route answers 404. Correct for an environment with no provider configured.

jobs.title: Scheduled jobs
jobs.body: The only thing that drains the email queue and expires holds. Without JOB_SECRET the endpoints refuse every caller, and the symptom is not an error — it is email that never arrives.

webhook.title: Mailgun webhook
webhook.body: How a bounce reaches the registration it belongs to. Without the signing key, requests are refused and delivery state stays unknown.

mapLink.title: Map link

Devs.rateLimitsIntro: How many attempts each guarded action accepts in a fixed window, per key — an email identity, a registration, one email link, or one job. A limit somebody is hitting looks like "the site is broken" without anything being broken.
Devs.rolesIntro: Each role can do everything the one below it can, plus one thing more. The line that matters is between Technical and Admin: from there up, participant data is visible.

roleSummary.DEV: plus the configuration page. No participant data

Devs.settingsIntro: Every value each setting accepts, with the one this deployment uses highlighted. Read from the same list the process validates against, so it cannot drift.
Devs.emailVolumeIntro: Three messages per completed registration, against the provider's daily allowance. Check this before opening a registration window, not after. Counted from midnight UTC.

APP_ENV.what: Which deployment this is. It — not NODE_ENV — decides every environment-dependent rule: whether live email may be sent, whether the development sign-in switcher is permitted, and whether sample legal text and test registrations may exist at all.

values.local: A developer's own machine. Email is captured and never transmitted; the sign-in switcher is available; sample legal text is seeded.
values.test: The automated suites. Same guarantees as local, and nothing here ever reaches a person.
values.qa: The shared deployment colleagues try things on. Real database, real sign-in, and email either captured or restricted to an allowlist — never open delivery.
values.production: The club's real site. The only environment permitted to send live email, and the only one that refuses sample legal text and test registrations outright.

EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE.what: How far a message actually goes once the outbox renders it. This is the guard between a test system and a stranger's inbox, and startup refuses any combination that would cross it.

values.capture: Nothing is transmitted. Messages are held in memory — which on a deployed serverless host means they reach nobody at all, so registration looks broken to anyone but a developer.
values.allowlist: Real delivery, but only to the addresses in EMAIL_ALLOWLIST; everything else is captured. This is what a Mailgun sandbox domain is, and it is how a small closed group tests the whole journey safely.
values.live: Real delivery to whoever registered. Permitted only when APP_ENV is production; stating it anywhere else fails at startup.

STAFF_AUTH_MODE.what: How a member of staff proves who they are. Participants never sign in at all — this is the backoffice door only, and the staff_users table decides who may come through it regardless of which mode is set.

values.dev-switcher: A local shortcut that lets a developer become any role without an identity provider. Permitted only when APP_ENV is local or test; stating it elsewhere fails at startup.
values.provider: The real thing: Auth.js with Zitadel. The provider proves the address, and the staff_users allowlist decides whether that address may in.
values.disabled: There is no way in. Every staff route answers 404 rather than a refusal, so the backoffice is unreachable rather than merely hidden. This is the correct setting for any environment with no identity provider configured.
